title: 2 Samuel 13:1–14
context: 2 Samuel 13 begins the sorrows Nathan foretold when he told David that the sword would not depart from his house and that evil would rise from within it (12:10–12). David’s son Amnon develops an obsessive desire for his half-sister Tamar. His friend Jonadab devises a deception, David unknowingly sends Tamar to Amnon’s house, and Amnon, refusing to listen to her clear and courageous resistance, rapes her. The narrative states the act briefly. Tamar is the victim; the guilt is Amnon’s, with Jonadab complicit. Both traditions read the passage soberly and as shared ground.

verses.text: After this, Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar; and Amnon the son of David loved her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom has a sister named Tamar, and her half-brother Amnon ‘loved’ her. The narrator introduces the people and the danger plainly.

Arminian readers note that what follows shows this was not love but self-centered desire. The story opens the sorrows foretold in 12:10–12.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘After this’ links the episode to David’s sin with Bathsheba and Nathan’s word that evil would rise from his own house.

Reformed readers see that judgment begin to unfold. Both traditions read this soberly, with Tamar as a person, not a plot device.

verses.text: Amnon was so troubled that he became sick because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed hard to Amnon to do anything to her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon becomes sick with desire, because Tamar is a virgin and it seems impossible to do anything to her. His obsession is already dangerous.

Arminian readers see desire nursed rather than resisted, moving toward sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator exposes Amnon’s inner state without excusing it. Tamar is protected by her status and the household’s norms.

Reformed readers see the heart’s corruption, as James 1:14–15 describes desire giving birth to sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground and place responsibility wholly on Amnon.

verses.text: But Amnon had a friend whose name was Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David’s brother; and Jonadab was a very subtle man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon’s friend Jonadab, David’s nephew, is described as ‘a very subtle man.’ Cleverness is about to serve evil.

Arminian readers see how counsel from the wrong friend can enable sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonadab’s shrewdness is not wisdom. The narrator signals that his skill will be misused.

Reformed readers see complicity beginning with a friend who should have restrained Amnon. Both traditions read this as shared ground, naming Jonadab’s role plainly as part of the wrong done to Tamar.

verses.text: He said to him, “Why, son of the king, are you so sad from day to day? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonadab asks why the king’s son looks so troubled; Amnon says he ‘loves’ Tamar. He names her as Absalom’s sister, not his own.

Arminian readers see Amnon distancing himself from the relationship that should have protected her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon’s wording avoids calling Tamar his sister. Jonadab now knows his intent.

Reformed readers see a confidant who hears and does not rebuke. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with moral clarity that Jonadab had the chance to warn and chose otherwise.

verses.text: Jonadab said to him, “Lay down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, tell him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonadab tells Amnon to pretend to be sick and ask David to send Tamar to prepare food in his sight. He designs the trap.

Arminian readers name this counsel as complicity in the harm that follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plan uses the king’s care for his son and Tamar’s kindness. Deception is its core.

Reformed readers see sin multiplying through shared schemes. Both traditions agree that Jonadab’s advice makes him complicit, and neither treats his cleverness as anything but a means to wrongdoing.

verses.text: So Amnon lay down and faked being sick. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make me a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon lies down, fakes illness, and asks the king to let Tamar make cakes in his sight. The deception reaches David.

Arminian readers see Amnon deliberately carrying out the plan. He is fully responsible for his choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon repeats Jonadab’s words to the king. The request appears innocent.

Reformed readers see how evil can disguise itself as ordinary need. Both traditions read this as shared ground and place the guilt on Amnon and his counselor, not on those deceived.

verses.text: Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, “Go now to your brother Amnon’s house, and prepare food for him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David sends Tamar to Amnon’s house to prepare food for him. The king unknowingly sends his daughter into danger.

Arminian readers see David failing to discern what was happening in his own house.
verses.reformedNotes:
David acts on the request without suspicion. The narrative does not say he knew Amnon’s intent.

Reformed readers see the king’s household vulnerable after his own sin. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, recognizing that Tamar obeys her father in good faith and bears no blame.

verses.text: So Tamar went to her brother Amnon’s house; and he was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked the cakes.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar goes to Amnon’s house and prepares cakes in his sight. She serves her brother with care and diligence.

Arminian readers see Tamar acting with kindness and obedience. Her conduct is honorable throughout.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator describes her work in detail, showing her integrity and good will.

Reformed readers likewise honor Tamar’s faithful service. Both traditions read this as shared ground and insist that nothing in her conduct invites the wrong done to her; the responsibility belongs entirely to Amnon.

verses.text: She took the pan and poured them out before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, “Have all men leave me.” Then every man went out from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar sets the food before Amnon, but he refuses to eat and orders everyone out. He isolates her.

Arminian readers see deliberate preparation for wrongdoing. Amnon removes any witnesses, and the responsibility is his alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refusal and dismissal reveal that the illness was a pretext. Tamar is left alone with him.

Reformed readers see sin seeking concealment. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, noting how the narrator shows Amnon’s planning step by step without excusing any of it.

verses.text: Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the room, that I may eat from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes which she had made, and brought them into the room to Amnon her brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon tells Tamar to bring the food into the inner room so he can eat from her hand. She does so in trust.

Arminian readers see Tamar acting innocently, while Amnon abuses that trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tamar brings the food as asked. She has no reason to suspect harm from her brother.

Reformed readers see a betrayal of family trust. Both traditions read this as shared ground and honor Tamar’s innocence, placing the coming wrong squarely on Amnon’s choices and Jonadab’s counsel.

verses.text: When she had brought them near to him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, “Come, lie with me, my sister!”
verses.arminianNotes:
When she brings the food, Amnon seizes her and demands that she lie with him. His intent is now open.

Arminian readers see the moment when concealed desire becomes violent action. Tamar is the victim.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon uses force from the start. The narrator reports this briefly and without elaboration.

Reformed readers see the depth of human sin when desire rules. Both traditions read this with sober clarity and treat Tamar with dignity as one wronged, not as a participant.

verses.text: She answered him, “No, my brother, do not force me! For no such thing ought to be done in Israel. Don’t you do this folly!
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar answers, “No, my brother, do not force me! For no such thing ought to be done in Israel. Don’t you do this folly!” She resists clearly.

Arminian readers honor her courage and moral clarity. Her words echo Genesis 34:7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tamar appeals to God’s standards for Israel and names the act as folly. She speaks with wisdom under threat.

Reformed readers likewise honor her voice. Both traditions read her words as a clear, righteous refusal that leaves no doubt about where guilt lies.

verses.text: As for me, where would I carry my shame? And as for you, you will be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king; for he will not withhold me from you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar asks where she could carry her shame and warns that Amnon would be like the fools in Israel; she urges him to ask the king. She seeks any way out.

Arminian readers see her reasoning to protect herself and even to restrain him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Leviticus 18:9 forbids such a union; interpreters differ on whether Tamar expected the king to permit it or was trying to escape.

Reformed readers likewise hold this open. Both traditions honor her resistance and dignity, and read her plea as an attempt to stop the wrong.

verses.text: However, he would not listen to her voice; but being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her.
verses.arminianNotes:
He would not listen to her voice, but being stronger, he forced her. The text states the act briefly, and these notes do not elaborate.

Arminian readers name it plainly as rape, a grave sin for which Amnon alone is responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon’s refusal to listen and his use of strength are the narrator’s focus. Tamar did not consent.

Reformed readers see the full guilt resting on Amnon. Both traditions agree that Tamar bears no blame; Deuteronomy 22:25–27 likewise holds a forced woman innocent.
